title: One Spirit, Many Gifts, One Body
summary: Paul begins his answer about spiritual gifts. The true sign of the Spirit is the confession that Jesus is Lord, and the Spirit gives a variety of gifts to each believer for the common good. Using the image of the human body, he teaches that the church needs every member, that no gift makes one member superior, and that the weaker and less honored parts deserve special care.
story: The question of spiritual gifts occupies chapters 12 to 14, the second half of Paul's teaching on the church's worship that began in 11:2. The Corinthians apparently prized speaking in tongues as the mark of a truly spiritual person, and their gatherings had become competitive and disorderly. Paul does not start with tongues. He starts with the Spirit's unity and the church's diversity (chapter 12), moves to love as the way all gifts must be used (chapter 13), and only then gives specific instructions about tongues and prophecy (chapter 14). The chapter continues the letter's constant theme: a church divided by status (chapters 1 to 4, 11) needs to see itself as one body in Christ.
historical:
The Corinthian believers had mostly been pagans (verse 2), familiar with religious experiences in which a god was thought to seize a worshiper: the prophetess at Delphi, across the Gulf of Corinth, spoke in a state of inspiration, and the cults of Dionysus and others valued ecstatic frenzy. Paul reminds them that they had been “led astray to mute idols,” and that ecstasy alone proves nothing. What marks the Holy Spirit's presence is the content of speech, above all the confession that Jesus is Lord.

The image of a community as a body was well known. The Roman historian Livy tells how the patrician Menenius Agrippa persuaded rebelling common people to return to Rome with a fable of the body's members revolting against the stomach, and Stoic philosophers described the universe and the city as a body. Such speeches were usually used to keep lower classes in their place. Paul turns the image around: the weaker, less honored members receive greater honor (verses 22 to 24).
cultural:
Status distinctions ran through every part of Corinthian life: slave and free, Jew and Greek, patron and client (verse 13 names two of these pairs). Gifts could easily become new badges of rank. Speaking in tongues, dramatic and audible, may have signaled higher spiritual standing, as rhetorical skill signaled social standing. Paul's list of gifts deliberately mixes the spectacular (miracles, tongues) with the ordinary (helping, administration, verse 28), and his rhetorical questions in verses 29 and 30 expect the answer no: not everyone has any one gift.

“Jesus is Lord” (verse 3) was the church's earliest confession, and it had political weight in a city where Caesar was hailed as lord. The strange phrase “Jesus be cursed” is debated: it may be a hypothetical contrast, a phrase heard in synagogue opposition to Christians, or something said in ecstatic speech that the Corinthians tolerated because it sounded inspired.
literary: Paul opens with “Now about” (verse 1), marking another answer to the Corinthians' letter. Verses 4 to 6 form a threefold parallel, gifts from the same Spirit, ministries from the same Lord, workings from the same God, one of the New Testament's clearest Trinitarian patterns. A list of nine manifestations follows (verses 8 to 10), framed by “the same Spirit.” The body analogy (verses 12 to 26) is developed with humor: a foot that sulks because it isn't a hand, an eye that tells the hand it isn't needed, a body that is one giant ear. The chapter ends with a ranked list (first apostles, second prophets, third teachers), a set of questions, and a bridge to chapter 13.

outline.t: The test of the Spirit: Jesus is Lord
The Spirit's gifts for the common good
One body baptized in one Spirit
The body of Christ and its gifts

doctrines.note: The Holy Spirit is personal and sovereign, apportioning gifts “to each one as He determines” (verse 11). Every believer has received the Spirit (verse 13), and every believer has been given some manifestation of the Spirit for others' benefit (verse 7).

Verses 4 to 6 speak of the same Spirit, the same Lord (Jesus), and the same God (the Father) at work in the church's gifts. Paul is not writing a doctrine of the Trinity, but his instinct to speak of God's work in this threefold way is part of the ground the later creeds built on.

“You are the body of Christ, and each of you is a member of it” (verse 27). The church is one organism, not a collection of spiritual individuals; its unity comes from the Spirit, and its diversity is God's design (verse 18).

words.note: Charisma, a gift of grace, from charis, grace. Five times here it names what the Spirit gives. The word stresses that gifts are free gifts, not rewards or proofs of spiritual superiority, and Paul used the same word in 7:7 for marriage and singleness.

Phanerosis, a manifestation, a making visible. “To each one the manifestation of the Spirit is given for the common good” (verse 7). Gifts are the Spirit becoming visible in the church through ordinary people, and their purpose is the good of others.

Melos, a member or limb of the body. Used thirteen times in the chapter, it carries the body analogy. Members are not interchangeable and not independent; each belongs to the others. English uses member for joining a club, but Paul means something far more organic.

Glossa, tongue, meaning both the physical organ and a language. Speaking in tongues is listed last in both lists (verses 10 and 28), probably not to belittle it but to correct the Corinthians' overvaluing of it. Chapter 14 discusses the gift at length.

christ: Paul makes Christ's lordship the test of true spiritual speech: “no one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except by the Holy Spirit” (verse 3). The Spirit's work is to glorify Jesus, not to produce impressive experiences. The church is not only like a body; it is “the body of Christ” (verse 27), joined to him and animated by his Spirit. Just as the crucified Christ was the weak and dishonored one whom God raised and honored, God gives greater honor to the members who seem weaker (verse 24). The shape of the church reflects the shape of the cross.

hard.q: Are the miraculous gifts, such as prophecy, tongues, and healing, still given today?
hard.a:
Christians who share the same confession about the Holy Spirit answer this in three main ways. Cessationists (common in Reformed and some Baptist traditions) hold that the revelatory and sign gifts, such as apostleship, prophecy, and tongues, served to establish the church and confirm the apostles' message, and ceased once the New Testament was complete; they often point to Ephesians 2:20 (the foundation of apostles and prophets) and to the history of the church, where such gifts were less prominent. Continuationists (including Pentecostal and charismatic churches, now a very large part of world Christianity, and many others) hold that all the gifts in this chapter continue until Christ returns, noting that the New Testament never says they will stop before then and that 13:8-12 ties their end to seeing face to face. A third, open-but-cautious position holds that nothing in Scripture rules out any gift today, but urges careful testing, stresses the sufficiency of Scripture, and is wary of claims that make particular experiences a mark of spiritual rank.

All three positions agree with what this chapter plainly teaches: the Spirit gives gifts to every believer, the gifts are for the common good, no gift makes anyone superior, and the confession of Jesus as Lord is the test of true spiritual speech. Related questions, such as whether being baptized in the Spirit (verse 13) happens at conversion for every believer or can also describe a later experience, likewise divide faithful churches. These are second-order questions.

questions: Which members of your church are least visible or least honored? What would it look like to give them greater honor, as Paul says God does?
Have you ever felt like the foot that says “I do not belong to the body”? What does this chapter say to that feeling?
If every gift is given for the common good, how are you using what you have been given for others?
